title: Potential Liability for Physicians Using Artificial Intelligence
author: W. Nicholson Price II · Sara Gerke · I. Glenn Cohen

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s context-specific, human-accountability framing and materially extends it into medical liability: AI accuracy alone does not determine legal responsibility, which instead depends on the standard of care, practitioner action and institutional context. It also broadens governance beyond the individual professional to hospitals, AI manufacturers and potentially payers.
qs: | Scenario | AI recommendation | AI accuracy | Physician action | Patient outcome | Legal outcome (probable) | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Standard of care | Correct | Follows | Good | No injury and no liability | | 2 | Standard of care | Correct | Rejects | Bad | Injury and liability | | 3 | Standard of care | Incorrect (standard of care is incorrect) | Follows | Bad | Injury but no liability |

Hospital systems that purchase and implement medical AI, makers of medical AI, and potentially even payers could all face liability.<sup>5</sup> The scenarios outlined in the Figure and the fundamental questions highlighted here recur and interact for each of these forms of liability.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between nominal human accountability and effective control: physicians remain legally exposed and formally retain discretion, yet opaque or fallible AI and malpractice incentives may discourage clinically valuable departures from standard care. Its analysis is predictive, however, because medical-AI case law was essentially absent.
qs: > The challenge is that current law incentivizes physicians to minimize the potential value of AI.
In this example, the physician retains this discretion, although in the future a health system or a payer may limit physician discretion.

kp.k: Clinical AI introduces opacity and potential patient injury
kp.d: The authors describe FDA-approved or cleared products and increasing hospital deployment of AI for clinical decisions, including drug selection, dosage and radiological interpretation. Some systems cannot explain their recommendations. Inappropriate training environments, imperfect techniques and incomplete data can cause errors, but even well-trained algorithms may injure patients. These are claims about medical practice, not findings about legal-service delivery.
qs: Multiple AI-based products have now been approved or cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and health systems and hospitals are increasingly deploying AI-based systems.

One key difference from most traditional clinical decision support software is that some medical AI may communicate results or recommendations to the care team without being able to communicate the underlying reasons for those results.
Medical AI may be trained in inappropriate environments, using imperfect techniques, or on incomplete data.

kp.k: Liability analysis extrapolates from tort principles, not AI precedents
kp.d: This 2019 Viewpoint offers a prospective interpretation of US physician liability under then-current law, rather than an empirical study or settled account of AI-specific judgments. Its baseline is the care expected of a competent physician in the same specialty, adjusted for available resources; the authors acknowledge essentially no medical-AI liability case law.
qs: In general, to avoid medical malpractice liability, physicians must provide care at the level of a competent physician within the same specialty, taking into account available resources.
In part because AI is so new to clinical practice, there is essentially no case law on liability involving medical AI.
Nonetheless, it is possible to understand how current law may be likely to treat these situations from more general tort law principles.

kp.k: Standard-of-care compliance matters more than patient-specific AI accuracy
kp.d: An eight-scenario hypothetical distinguishes AI recommendation, accuracy, physician response, patient outcome and probable liability. It assumes bevacizumab at 15 mg/kg every 3 weeks is standard care for an ovarian-cancer patient, versus a nonstandard 75 mg/kg every 3 weeks that could hypothetically be correct for that patient. In this explicitly stylized model, no injury means no liability; following standard care generally avoids liability despite injury, whereas departing from it and causing injury creates liability exposure. The dosage example is illustrative, not clinical evidence or a treatment recommendation.
qs: Assume the standard of care for this patient would be to administer 15 mg/kg every 3 weeks of the chemotherapeutic bevacizumab.
Even though 15 mg/kg every 3 weeks is the standard-of-care dosage, perhaps for some reason the higher dosage is right for this particular patient.
First, if there is no injury, there will be no liability (green boxes in the Figure)
Second, tort law typically privileges the standard of care, regardless of its effectiveness in a particular case—ie, whether providing that care leads to a good or bad outcome.

kp.k: Liability incentives favor confirmation over AI-enabled improvement
kp.d: The authors argue that standard-of-care protection makes confirmatory AI use the safest liability strategy, potentially discouraging beneficial personalized departures. They condition this concern on AI performing a task better than physicians and offering different recommendations; superiority to even the best physicians is described as a future possibility and algorithmic goal, not an established finding.
qs: This analysis suggests an important implication for physicians using medical AI to aid their clinical decisions: because current law shields physicians from liability as long as they follow the standard of care, the "safest" way to use medical AI from a liability perspective is as a confirmatory tool to support existing decision-making processes, rather than as a source of ways to improve care.

But because threat of liability encourages physicians to meet and follow the standard of care, they may reject such recommendations and thus fail to realize the full value of AI, in some cases to patients' detriment.

kp.k: AI adoption could eventually alter the standard of care
kp.d: The authors predict conditionally that, if AI becomes part of accepted good medical practice, physicians might become liable for rejecting correct recommendations that previously counted as nonstandard, while following incorrect AI recommendations might become defensible. They expect protection for AI-supported departures to emerge before liability for rejecting AI, citing tort law's conservatism. They specify no adoption date.
qs: The legal standard of care is key to liability for medical AI, but it is not forever fixed.

If and when that happens, scenarios 6 and 7 (italicized text in the Figure) may change substantially: physicians may incur liability for rejecting correct but nonstandard AI recommendations and may conversely avoid liability for injury if they were following incorrect AI recommendations.

Because tort law is inherently conservative, the second alternative (scenario 7) is a more likely first step: reliance on medical AI to deviate from the otherwise known standard of care will likely be a defense to liability well before physicians are held liable for rejecting AI recommendations.

kp.k: Physicians need AI interpretation skills and professional guidance
kp.d: The authors recommend learning when an algorithm is applicable and how much confidence its recommendation deserves, while acknowledging immature evaluation tools. They urge professional societies to evaluate practice-specific algorithms and supplement FDA review with implementation and patient-level guidance, analogous to societies' existing role in shaping intervention standards.
qs: In their practices, physicians should learn how to better use and interpret AI algorithms, including in what situations an available medical AI should be applied and how much confidence should be placed in an algorithmic recommendation.
This is a challenge, and evaluation tools are still very much under development.

Review by the FDA will provide some quality assurance, but societies will be well placed to provide additional guidelines to evaluate AI products at implementation and to evaluate AI recommendations for individual patients.

kp.k: Clinical oversight should shape deployment and procurement
kp.d: The authors recommend physician involvement to ensure institutional algorithm development and deployment meet clinical needs, and rigorous vetting before buying external products. Their liability hypothetical assumes physicians retain discretion to reject AI recommendations, but they identify possible future constraints imposed by health systems or payers.
qs: In this example, the physician retains this discretion, although in the future a health system or a payer may limit physician discretion.

As part of care settings, such as in hospitals and health systems, physicians should also ensure that administrative efforts to develop and deploy algorithms reflect what is truly needed in clinical care.
When external AI products are procured, physicians should advocate for safeguards to ensure that such products are rigorously vetted before procurement, just as with other novel medical devices.

kp.k: Malpractice coverage requires scrutiny as AI use expands
kp.d: Physicians are advised to check whether insurers distinguish AI-supported care from other care, including whether opacity affects coverage. These are questions for investigation, not reported findings about insurance practices. The authors suggest collective physician and hospital action could seek coverage terms suited to AI-enabled medicine.
qs: In addition, physicians should check carefully with their malpractice insurer to determine how the insurer covers the use of medical AI in practice.
Are practices different for more opaque algorithms that provide little or no reasoning?
Collectively, physicians and their hospital systems may be able to make demands for changes in terms of insurance coverage to better accommodate the needs of a future of AI-enabled medicine.

kp.k: Liability extends beyond physicians and could undergo legislative redesign
kp.d: The authors identify hospitals, AI manufacturers and potentially payers as additional actors exposed to liability, with interacting questions beyond the physician-focused model. Alongside gradual evolution of standards of care, they raise legislation establishing a vaccine-injury-style no-fault system as a possible alternative, not an enacted AI regime or a definite prediction.
qs: Hospital systems that purchase and implement medical AI, makers of medical AI, and potentially even payers could all face liability.
The scenarios outlined in the Figure and the fundamental questions highlighted here recur and interact for each of these forms of liability.

Moreover, the law may change; in addition to AI becoming the standard of care, which may happen through ordinary legal evolution, legislatures could impose very different rules, such as a no-fault system like the one that currently compensates individuals who have vaccine injuries.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Price, Gerke and Cohen describe growing clinical adoption of AI, alongside opacity, errors and potential patient injuries.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about medicine and physician liability, not legal-service delivery. The authors state that medical AI supports drug and dosage recommendations and radiological interpretation. Some systems cannot explain their recommendations. Inappropriate training environments, imperfect techniques and incomplete data can cause errors, but even well-trained algorithms can make harmful recommendations.

pts.k: The authors predict that existing malpractice incentives favor using AI to confirm conventional care rather than to pursue potentially superior personalized treatment.
pts.d: In their simplified analysis of US tort law, injury is necessary for liability, and following the standard of care generally protects physicians even when another treatment would have benefited the patient. Departing from that standard and causing injury exposes physicians to liability. Consequently, physicians may reject beneficial nonstandard AI recommendations. The authors identify this as a potential impediment to realizing AI's clinical value, not as an empirically demonstrated behavioral effect.

pts.k: If AI becomes part of the standard of care, the authors predict that liability protections and obligations could shift toward reliance on AI.
pts.d: The authors conditionally suggest that physicians could become liable for rejecting correct recommendations that depart from the otherwise conventional standard, while avoiding liability for injuries from following incorrect AI recommendations. They predict an asymmetric transition: using AI as a defense for a departure from conventional care is likely to precede liability for rejecting AI advice. They also identify legislative replacement of existing liability arrangements, such as a vaccine-injury-style no-fault compensation system, as a possibility rather than a forecast of enactment.

pts.k: The authors anticipate new clinical governance responsibilities and a liability ecosystem extending beyond physicians.
pts.d: Their recommendations include physician education in appropriate AI use and interpretation, professional-society evaluation and guidance, rigorous procurement safeguards, and checking malpractice coverage. These are prescriptions rather than findings that such practices already prevail. They suggest that collective physician and hospital action may reshape insurance coverage, and that hospitals, AI makers and potentially payers could also face liability. Whether insurers currently treat AI-dependent or opaque systems differently is posed as a question, not established as a fact.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The central liability claims derive from general tort principles and a stylized hypothetical, not medical-AI case outcomes or performance data.
pts.d: The authors explicitly acknowledge essentially no medical-AI liability case law at publication. Their eight-scenario illustration varies standard versus nonstandard recommendations, correctness, physician acceptance and injury, using hypothetical bevacizumab dosages of 15 versus 75 mg/kg every three weeks. It illustrates probable legal outcomes rather than testing clinical efficacy or reporting actual injuries. Supporting authorities include Topol on medical AI adoption, Burrell on opacity, Froomkin, Kerr and Pineau on AI and the standard of care, and Price on black-box medicine and malpractice. The article provides no quantitative adoption estimates, model benchmarks or measured physician responses to liability incentives.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The baseline is US law as discussed in October 2019; future changes are conditional and have no specified dates.
pts.d: The article was published online October 4, 2019. Its current-law analysis assumes physician discretion and a simplified relationship between recommendation correctness and patient outcome. Future liability changes depend on AI becoming accepted as part of good medical practice or on legislative intervention. AI outperforming even the best physicians is described as a future possibility and an algorithm-development goal, not an established capability. The authors also suggest that health systems or payers might eventually constrain physician discretion. Their timing language is qualitative: liability issues may arise soon and legal standards may change quickly.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected parties are physicians, patients, healthcare institutions, professional societies, AI makers, payers and malpractice insurers.
pts.d: Physicians face decisions about reliance on AI, potential malpractice exposure and new learning needs. Patients may receive better personalized treatment, suffer AI-related injury, or lose potential benefits when liability incentives discourage departures from conventional care. Hospitals and health systems face procurement, deployment and possible liability responsibilities. Professional societies can help shape standards for adoption and patient-specific use. AI makers and potentially payers may share liability exposure; payers or health systems may also restrict clinical discretion. Insurers' treatment of AI use becomes an issue for physicians and institutions to investigate and potentially negotiate. The source makes no direct claims about legal jobs, law-firm staffing or legal-service markets.
